questions.question: Compare a transit and an occultation by apparent angular size, and say whether viewing location can matter.

facts.claim: A transiting body looks smaller than the background body and blocks only part of it.

sources.quote: another celestial body of larger angular size

A transit can be absent from a different line of sight.

sources.quote: may not be seen by another observer

questions.question: Use “How astronomers detect exoplanets” to compare what transit depth and radial velocity tell you, and what combining them adds.
questions.expected: Three claims using the named article, with the limits of each technique.

facts.claim: Transit depth constrains radius ratio squared; a stellar radius is needed for planet radius.
Radial velocity typically constrains minimum mass.
Transit inclination improves mass, or mass and radius together give mean density.
